Shippers stated that motor carrier operations within the present exempt zone are orderly, and it is not expected that expansion of the zone should alter that fact. It was urged that the zone be expanded so shippers would benefit from an increase in available service options and carriers would benefit from larger service areas.
We continue to adhere to the interim decision to restore the exemption of section 203(b)(8) to New York City for the reasons stated in the Interim Report, Commercial Zones, 124 M.C.C. at 176-77. The comments we have received do not refute the economic findings of the Interim Report. Opponents of the change argue that the potential effects are serious and adverse. We will discuss those contentions in a later section of this report. Certain parties assert that application of the section 203(b)(8) exemption to New York City is inappropriate, since the volume of traffic in that area is immense and of great economic significance. We do not find in the statute, however, any "economic significance" test governing the imposition or removal of the commercial zone exemption. Nor can such a test be found by analogy with other exemptions from our regulation, for some exemptions from our regulation are of substantial economic importance. For example, the agricultural exemption 
(\frac{7}{2}03(b)(6))
, bulk water movements 
(\overline{3}03(b))
, and private carriage have significant economic impact on the national transportation system.
